title: Taifa of Badajoz
capsule: The Taifa of Badajoz emerged after the collapse of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba c. 1009–1013 as one of the petty successor kingdoms of al-Andalus, founded by the Aftasid dynasty under Sabur al-Saqlabi (a former slave official) and consolidated by his son Abdullah ibn Maslamah. At its height the kingdom encompassed most of Extremadura and parts of Portugal and León, including the towns of Mérida and Évora. The Aftasids navigated shifting alliances with León and Castile while paying parias (tribute) to buy protection; Ibn al-Aftas's cultural court was celebrated for poetry. The Almoravid invasion ended the taifa system: the Almoravid ruler Yusuf ibn Tashfin annexed Badajoz in 1094, though brief resistance continued until 1095.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Aftasid political history is reasonably well documented in Arabic chronicles; precise frontier zones between Badajoz and neighboring taifas and Christian kingdoms shifted frequently and are incompletely mapped.
